Consider the matrices above. Given that $A = P J P^{-1}$ is a Jordan canonical decomposition of $A,$ find the second column of the matrix $P.$
examples.worked_solution:
From the Jordan matrix $J,$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are 

$$
\lambda_1=\lambda_2=4.
$$

As a result, we obtain that 

- the first column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070862/assets/9bff79e13c06645253e57b8e6f43689c7ce21ac818c3ffdc677e03b5a9b08eb7.png) of the eigenvalue $\lambda=4,$

- the second column of $P$ corresponds to the vector $\mathbf{v}_2$ such that $(A-4I)\mathbf{v}_2 = \mathbf{v}_1.$

Now, computing $A-4I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}9 & 5 \\ -5 & -1\end{aligned}]-(4)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 5 \\ -5 & -5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, the matrix equation $(A - 4I)\mathbf{v}_2 = \mathbf{v}_1$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 5 & -1 \\ -5 & -5 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}5 & 5 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, $x_2$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain $x_1=-\dfrac 15 - x_2.$ Hence, the general solution is

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070862/assets/44f1c49ffc09942f7062c8e4da4419a214551cdf659ee92be03556c52a2f3005.png)

Therefore, setting $x_2=0,$ we get

feedback.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}11 & -8 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}],\,J=[\begin{aligned}7 & 1 \\ 0 & 7\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}a & ∗ \\ b & ∗\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices above. Given that $A=PJ{P}^{-1}$ is a Jordan canonical decomposition of $A,$ find the value of $\frac{b}{a}.$
feedback.worked_solution:
From the Jordan matrix $J,$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=7.
$$

As a result, the first column of $P$ corresponds to an eigenvector of the eigenvalue $\lambda =7.$ 

Now, computing $A-7I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-7I & =[\begin{aligned}11 & -8 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}]-(7)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -8 \\ 2 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -8 & 0 \\ 2 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}4 & -8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=2{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{b}{a}=\frac{1}{2}.$
